at nyse.explanation: "At nyse" means "to sneeze": Jeg nyser hele tiden (I sneeze all the time).

sentence.da: Jeg er forkølet og må **nyse** hele tiden.
sentence.en: I have a cold and have to sneeze all the time.

en nabo.explanation: "En nabo" means "a neighbor", for a man or a woman. You can ask Kender du dine naboer? (Do you know your neighbors?).

sentence.en: My neighbor lives next door.

en nat.explanation: "En nat" means "a night". Common phrases are i nat (tonight or last night), om natten (at night) and godnat (good night).

sentence.en: I sleep eight hours every night.
She is wearing a blue skirt.

en negl.explanation: "En negl" means "a nail" on a finger or toe. A metal nail you hit with a hammer is a different word, et søm (a metal nail), so do not mix them up.

sentence.da: Jeg har knækket en **negl** på min finger.
sentence.en: I have broken a nail on my finger.

en næse.explanation: "En næse" means "a nose". You can say Jeg har en løbende næse (I have a runny nose).

sentence.da: Jeg kan lugte blomsten med min **næse**.
sentence.en: I can smell the flower with my nose.

en nøgle.explanation: "En nøgle" means "a key", for a door or a hotel room. You can ask Hvor er min nøgle? (Where is my key?).

sentence.en: I open the door with my key.

et navn.explanation: "Et navn" means "a name". To ask someone's name, Danes say Hvad hedder du?, literally What are you called?, or Hvad er dit navn? (What is your name?).

sentence.en: What is your name?

et nummer.explanation: "Et nummer" means "a number" used as a label, such as a phone number or a house number. For counting or amounts use et tal (a number, a figure) instead. Hvad er dit telefonnummer? means "What is your phone number?".

sentence.en: I call your number.

natur.explanation: "Natur" means "nature". It is used without en: smuk natur (beautiful nature).

sentence.en: Denmark has beautiful nature.

ned.explanation: "Ned" means "down", for moving down. Compare Kom ned! (Come down!) with Han er nede i kælderen (He is down in the cellar). Nede says where someone is, ned says where someone is going.

sentence.en: The elevator goes up and down.

nej.explanation: "Nej" means "no". It can also mean "oh!" when you are surprised: Nej, hvor er det flot! (Oh, how beautiful!).

sentence.en: Do you want coffee? No, thank you.

nem.explanation: "Nem" means "easy": en nem løsning (an easy solution).

sentence.en: The task is very easy.

nemt.explanation: "Nemt" means "easy" or "easily". Compare Det er nemt (It is easy) with Han vinder nemt (He wins easily).

sentence.da: Det er **nemt**: to plus to er fire.
sentence.en: It is easy: two plus two is four.

ni.explanation: "Ni" means "nine". Do not mix it up with nej (no): Jeg har ni børn (I have nine children) but Nej, tak (No, thank you).

sentence.en: After eight comes nine.

niende.explanation: "Niende" means "ninth": den niende dag (the ninth day). It is also used for dates: den niende maj (the ninth of May).

sentence.da: Efter den ottende dag kommer den **niende** dag.
sentence.en: After the eighth day comes the ninth day.

nitten.explanation: "Nitten" means "nineteen". Compare ni børn (nine children) with nitten børn (nineteen children).

sentence.en: My sister is nineteen years old.

nogen.explanation: "Nogen" means "someone" or "anyone": Jeg ser nogen (I see someone), Jeg ser ikke nogen (I do not see anyone). With more than one thing it means "any", in questions and with ikke: Har du nogen børn? (Do you have any children?), Jeg har ikke nogen venner (I do not have any friends).

sentence.en: There is nobody home.

noget.explanation: "Noget" means "something" or "anything". Compare Jeg ser noget (I see something) with Jeg ser nogen (I see someone): noget is for things, nogen is for people. With things you cannot count it means "some": noget mælk (some milk).

forms.da: Vil du have noget at spise?
forms.en: Do you want something to eat?

sentence.da: Jeg er tørstig. Har du **noget** at drikke?
sentence.en: I am thirsty. Do you have something to drink?

nogle.explanation: "Nogle" means "some" or "a few". Compare Jeg har en ven (I have one friend) with Jeg har nogle venner (I have some friends). In a question or with ikke, use nogen instead: Har du nogen venner? (Do you have any friends?).

sentence.en: There are some apples on the table.

nogle gange.explanation: "Nogle gange" means "sometimes", or word for word some times: Jeg spiser nogle gange morgenmad (I sometimes eat breakfast).

sentence.en: Sometimes I take the bus.

nok.explanation: "Nok" means "enough" and also "probably". Compare Jeg har nok mad (I have enough food) with Han kommer nok (He will probably come). The first is about how much, the second is a guess. Alone, Det er nok! (That is enough!) tells someone to stop.

sentence.en: No thanks, I have enough food.

nord.explanation: "Nord" means "north". Compare Det er koldt i nord (It is cold in the north) with Det er varmt i syd (It is warm in the south).

sentence.en: Norway lies to the north.

norge.explanation: "Norge" means "Norway". The country is Norge, but the language is norsk (Norwegian): Jeg bor i Norge og taler norsk (I live in Norway and speak Norwegian).

sentence.da: Min ven kommer fra **Norge** og taler norsk.
sentence.en: My friend comes from Norway and speaks Norwegian.

normal.explanation: "Normal" means "normal", the same word as in English: Det er helt normalt (That is completely normal).

sentence.da: I dag er en helt **normal** dag.
sentence.en: Today is a completely normal day.

norsk.explanation: "Norsk" means "Norwegian", both for things from Norway and for the language. Danish writes it with a small letter: Jeg taler norsk (I speak Norwegian).

sentence.da: Han bor i Norge og taler **norsk**.
sentence.en: He lives in Norway and speaks Norwegian.

november.explanation: "November" means "November". Danish writes month names with a small letter, even in the middle of a sentence: i november (in November).

sentence.da: Det er mørkt og gråt i **november**.
sentence.en: It is dark and grey in November.

nu.explanation: "Nu" means "now". Compare Jeg går nu (I am leaving now) with Jeg går senere (I am leaving later).

sentence.en: I have to go now.
I boil noodles in water.

nul.explanation: "Nul" means "zero". Compare Det er nul grader (It is zero degrees) with Det er ti grader (It is ten degrees). In sports it is also "nil": Vi vinder to–nul (We win two–nil).

sentence.da: Vandet bliver til is ved **nul** grader.
sentence.en: Water turns to ice at zero degrees.

ny.explanation: "Ny" means "new". It is also part of nytår (new year), as in godt nytår (happy new year).

sentence.en: I have bought a new phone.

nyheder.explanation: "Nyheder" means "news". Where English says the news is bad, Danish says nyhederne er dårlige, literally the news are bad, because the word is for more than one piece of news. One single piece of news is en nyhed.

sentence.da: Jeg læser **nyheder** i avisen hver morgen.
sentence.en: I read the news in the newspaper every morning.

nytårsaften.explanation: "Nytårsaften" means "New Year's Eve", the evening of 31 December. It is made from nytår (new year) and aften (evening).

sentence.da: På **nytårsaften** siger vi "godt nytår" ved midnat.
sentence.en: On New Year's Eve we say "happy new year" at midnight.

nå.explanation: "Nå" means "oh" or "well". You say it when you understand something or are a little surprised: Nå, jeg forstår (Oh, I see). Do not mix it up with nu (now).

sentence.en: Oh, now I understand it!

når.explanation: "Når" means "when" for things that happen every time or have not happened yet. Compare Når det regner, bliver jeg hjemme (Whenever it rains, I stay home) with Da jeg kom hjem, var det mørkt (When I came home, it was dark), which was one time in the past and uses da. In a question use hvornår: Hvornår kommer du? (When are you coming?).

sentence.en: I will call when I get home.

nær.explanation: "Nær" means "close" or "near". It is mostly used about people you are close to, like a friend or family member. For places, tæt på (close to) is more common: tæt på stationen means "close to the station".

sentence.da: Han er en **nær** ven af mig.
sentence.en: He is a close friend of mine.

næsten.explanation: "Næsten" means "almost". Compare Jeg er færdig (I am done) with Jeg er næsten færdig (I am almost done). Do not mix it up with næste (next): næste uge (next week).

sentence.en: I am almost done with the work.

nødt til.explanation: "Nødt til" means "have to" when you have no choice. It goes with at and an action: Jeg er nødt til at gå (I have to go). Compare it with Jeg vil gå (I want to go).

forms.da: jeg er nødt til at gå
du er nødt til at vente
vi er nødt til at tale

sentence.da: Jeg er **nødt til** at gå nu.
sentence.en: I have to go now.
